correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the six ordered-edge classes S,O,T,B,C,F from endpoint-geodesic alternatives, including conditional densities in the three intervals (0,1),(1,3/2),(3/2,2) and the identity q_C=(q_B+q_F)/2. Normalized counts sum to m^2, where m=(N^2-P2)/2. The density intercept 2/m, slope at zero, jump at 3/2 and left limit at 2 recover m,A=O+T,T,H=B+C/2. The algebraic identities 2A-T=2m(N-2), A=-N^3+4mN-2m+P3 and 2H=P4+N(N+1)P2-N^3-2NP3+2m recover all four powers. Newton identities prove <=4-part rigidity; s=(-9,-5,-1,7,8) has sum s and s^3 zero, giving the distinct positive five-part lists with identical first four powers. Independently enumerated all ordered-edge categories for 27 small multipartite examples and checked the collision powers; this is bounded corroboration, not proof for all part sizes. Endpoints of density are one-sided; sampling vertices has zero probability.

evidence: The Jin–Zhang theorem reconstructs multipartite graphs from the distance *matrix spectrum* on discrete vertices; this stronger/different observable cannot establish injectivity from a scalar arclength histogram. Mémoli–Needham study general metric-measure inverse questions but available material does not assert this all-part-size equivalence.
broader_coverage.reasoning: An inverse theorem based on richer input does not logically imply inversion from this poorer scalar input. Noninjectivity at five parts directly precludes general graph identification by the scalar law.

value.rationale: Global continuous two-point distance histograms are a natural, information-losing metric-graph invariant. Determining exactly what part-size information they encode is an inverse problem; four-moment recovery yields the sharp identification threshold, while explicit nonisomorphic five-part collisions show the limitation. Full distribution equivalence is strictly finer than a mean-only computation, and the collision is a motivated boundary, not an arbitrary small example.

final_claim: For unit-edge intrinsic complete multipartite metric graphs with at least two nonempty parts, equality of global normalized-arclength pairwise distance distributions is equivalent to equality of part-size power sums of degrees 1,2,3,4; the histogram identifies graphs with <=4 parts, but the two explicit five-part examples (1,5,9,17,18) and (2,3,11,15,19) collide.
limitations: Requires unit-length edges and normalized arclength, distinct continuous edge intervals and at least two positive integer parts.
